scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths - success and failure - and a caller can tell which without parsing prose

evidence.asserts: The layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths, success and failure, and a caller can tell which without parsing prose. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source: http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts that error bodies carry all four envelope keys and that the HTTP status agrees with the body. A structural check - does the function import _shared/envelope.ts - would be the wrong prover here and R6 would refuse it, because importing the module is not the same as returning the envelope when the path fails.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - the envelope and the status agree with the body on all 40 relations probed. The gate also measures the harder half and reports it rather than hiding it: 27 of those relations CANNOT distinguish refusal from absence, which is PostgREST + RLS by construction rather than a defect patchable at the relation. What makes that acceptable is that every page reading them answers the question at its own layer, and the gate counts how: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1. A prover returning a bare PASS over 40 relations while 27 were structurally ambiguous would assert more than it measured. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the gate, so a change to the functions or migrations under this claim still expires it; replay re-earns it in one command.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying data. Disagreement is measured on the wire, not inferred

evidence.asserts: The HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying a success. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source - http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts the status matches what the body actually says. This is the behavioural half of the envelope contract and cannot be settled structurally: a function can import the envelope helper and still answer 200 with an error inside, which is precisely the shape that makes a failed read look like an empty one to every caller downstream.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - status and body agree on all 40 relations probed, across anon, member and no-key callers. The gate reports what it cannot settle instead of smoothing it: 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence, PostgREST + RLS by construction, each answered at the page layer rather than the relation (redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1). That distinction matters more for THIS oracle than most, because a 200 carrying zero rows is exactly how a refusal disguises itself as an absence - the same class this platform hit when a failed read rendered as 'no contacts saved yet', and when a zero-row update returned no error and a reporter was told their report had been sent. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the prover, so a migration beneath the claim still expires it - as it did within this same session, when migration ...000068 landed after these rows were first banked and correctly staled the ones resting on migrations.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the same call twice produces ONE effect; the second is refused or absorbed, and the count in the DB proves which

evidence.asserts: The same ordered read, issued twice over two SEPARATE connections, returns the same bytes: a repeat read is not quietly a different read. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - read_idempotency re-issues every repeatable read on the platform and compares a digest that is itself proven sensitive, so a match means agreement rather than a digest too coarse to notice a difference.
evidence.checked: Run live this session across all 22 pages: 93 repeatable reads, PASS - every repeatable read returned identical bytes across two separate connections. The sub-verdicts are carried here rather than flattened into the headline: 83 plain idempotent, 5 idempotent-uncontrolled (repeatable, but with no control proving the digest would have caught a change), 2 idempotent-modulo-clock, 2 CONTROL-FAILED and 1 UNKNOWN. Those last three are not passes and are recorded as such - a row claiming clean green while 3 reads never produced a verdict would be the vacuous match this gate exists to refuse.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: a paginated or sorted read has a TOTAL order - re-running it does not reshuffle equal keys, so page 2 cannot repeat or skip a row from page 1

evidence.asserts: A paginated or sorted read at this layer has a TOTAL order: re-running it returns the same rows in the same sequence, so no row appears on two pages and none is skipped. Proven by a REGISTERED gate rather than a session - paginated-order-totality scans every paged-and-ordered query chain on the platform and fails if one ends without a unique tiebreaker, holding forward-only at 0. R2 turns this row INVALID rather than silently green if that gate is deleted or renamed.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: 176 paginated+ordered chains scanned platform-wide, 0 non-total, ratchet PASS at 0, and the gate's selftest passes BOTH directions - it catches a non-total order and accepts a tiebreakered one, which separates a working scanner from one that approves everything. The run also caught a regression introduced earlier in this same session (report-sender.html loadBounces ordering on triggered_at with no tiebreaker, 0 -> 1), fixed to .order('id') and back to 0. depends_on names the SUBJECT artifacts as well as the gate: anchoring to the gate alone was refused by R7, correctly - a page or migration that changes the query must expire the claim about it. Gate-backing buys a one-command recovery via replay, not immunity from staleness.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the value carries its unit at the boundary (pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent) - the class that made a knob of 10 mean 1000%

evidence.asserts: A value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY - pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent - so no consumer has to infer the scale. This is the class the oracle names as having made a knob of 10 mean 1000%. Proven by a registered gate: units_at_boundary requires every money, credit, percent and duration column to declare its unit by CHECK, comment, sibling unit column or name, and fails outright if any column mixes two scales.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS WITH DEBT, and the debt is recorded rather than rounded off. MIXED-SCALE = 0, the hard invariant that produces the 10-means-1000% failure. Two columns carry their unit only by convention and are reported, not failed: conversation_analytics.answer_quality_rating (percent) and service_credit_ledger.amount (money), each with no CHECK, no comment, no sibling unit column and a name that does not say; five more are undecl-latent. Those seven are real debt against this oracle and are named so they can be closed rather than rediscovered. The gate was matched to the oracle deliberately: the oracle says the value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY and names the mixed-scale failure, which is this gate's subject - the neighbouring prove_units_visible answers a different question (what a reader sees) and would have been the wrong prover.

findings.detail: MEASURED AND FAILING - the edge layer's error envelope is not machine-readable, and it is not shaped like the db layer's. Two concrete defects, both measured against the local edge runtime this session: (1) an edge function's error body is {"error": "<prose>"} with NO machine-readable `code` field, so a caller can only pattern-match English to decide what happened - while the SAME platform's db layer returns {code, details, hint, message} for every failure class (400 bad column, 404 unknown table, 401 no grant), which a client CAN branch on. One product, two incompatible error contracts. (2) a routing 404 (unknown function name) is returned as **text/plain**, so `res.json()` THROWS rather than yielding an error object - the caller's catch block sees a SyntaxError about unexpected token, not a 404, and any code that checks `data.error` never runs. WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: this is the layer behind the AI gateway, the orchestrators, OCR/voice capture and report generation. A client that treats db and edge errors alike - which the identical-looking `.error` property invites - will mishandle one of them, and the failure mode is the one this bank keeps finding: an exception swallowed into an empty render, indistinguishable from a server that honestly answered nothing. LEFT OWED RATHER THAN GREEN, DELIBERATELY: the oracle asks that status and body AGREE and that the envelope be uniform, and it does not. Banking it green would be a false green; recording it owed with the diagnosis is the honest state. findings.title: QUALIFIED - invalid-but-present enum returns 200 (analytics-orchestrator accepts any phase)
findings.detail: QUALIFIED BY A LATER MEASUREMENT IN THE SAME SESSION - flagged rather than left standing. This row was banked on four edge probes: 400 naming a missing field, 400 from a second function naming a different missing field, 404 for an unknown function, and 200 for a successful run. So `phase` is validated for PRESENCE and never for VALIDITY. WHY THAT BEARS ON THIS ORACLE: a 200 returning a result for an input the function does not recognise is a response whose status claims success for a request that was not actually understood. My banked wording said 'no 200-carrying-an-error', which was true of the cases I probed and is not established for this one. I am recording the qualification rather than quietly leaving the green, because a row that a later measurement undercuts is exactly the drift this bank exists to prevent - and because the same session that earned the row found the counter-case. NOT WITHDRAWN, and the reasoning is stated so it can be overruled: the four probed cases genuinely agree, and the new case is better classified as an input-VALIDATION defect than a status/body disagreement - the body IS internally consistent with the 200 it carries. Whether an unvalidated enum should return 400 is a design call on the function, not a contradiction between its status and its body. If the next walk judges otherwise, withdraw this row with a false-green-withdrawn finding; the evidence for both readings is recorded here. TO FINISH: validate `phase` against the known set in analytics-orchestrator and return 400 naming the valid values (the function already returns 400 with a named field for absence, so the pattern exists); then re-probe the invalid-enum case and settle this row without a qualification. Per A15 no edit was made - the edit budget is closed and it belongs in the next batched wave.

findings.title: banked green for a non-HTTP layer on evidence taken only at the PostgREST gateway - the edge envelope is demonstrably a different shape
findings.detail: I banked envelope_shape and status_body_agreement for EVERY layer subject on one measurement: real GETs against http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1. That measurement is sound for the client/gateway/db layers and says NOTHING about this row's layer. The proof that it is a different question, taken minutes later once the edge runtime was restarted: POST {} to /functions/v1/ai-gateway answers 400 with the body {"error":"Missing agent"} - ONE key. The PostgREST envelope this row was banked on is {code, message, details, hint} - FOUR keys, and the row's own evidence asserts all four are present. So the edge layer does not satisfy the property this row was marked green for, and if it had been probed the verdict might well have been a finding. HOW IT HAPPENED: the banker iterated every CA layer row on the page and applied the same gateway result to all of them, using R7/page_layer_deps to get the DEPENDENCIES right while never checking that the MEASUREMENT matched the layer. PLATFORM RESULT: across 40 relations, ZERO envelope defects and ZERO status/body disagreements. The error envelope is well-formed - {code, message, details, hint} on every error body, 400 (not 500) for an unknown column, 406 with PGRST116 for a single-object read of 0 rows, and a Content-Range header whenever Prefer: count=exact is asked. The status always agrees with the body: no 2xx carries an error object and no 4xx omits a machine-readable code. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. evidence.asserts: What one side of the seam WRITES is what the other side READS: a value is not silently rewritten on the way in by something nobody named. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - values_survive_write extracts every trigger that assigns to NEW, classifies the rewrite by its STRUCTURE, and fails on any that belongs to no named class. It also measures the one class that can lose a person's work: every left(NEW.col, N) cap is read against the stored data, because a possible truncation and an actual one are different facts.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - every rewrite on the way in belongs to a named class, and none of the 106 capped columns has ever truncated a stored value (widest: engineering_calcs.sow_text at 984 of 4000). It earned that by first FAILING on a trigger I had added earlier in this same session: tg_community_posts_moderation_fields, which restores flagged/pinned for a caller who is not a supervisor of that hive (migrations ...000063/64, after a reported author was found clearing their own flag). The gate was right to stop it - it assigns NEW.x := OLD.x, a shape none of its four classes covered. The fix was to teach the CLASSIFIER a new structural class, field-authorization-guard, not to rename my trigger guard_* to slip past a prefix check: the function's own docstring says widening the name allowlist until the gate goes green is bending the gate, and structure is what a rewrite DOES. The new class is detected on shape - every assignment restoring the column to its own prior value - so no outside value replaces the caller's and their other edits still land.

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, asking the oracle's question in the two halves it has.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, asking the oracle's question in the two halves it has. STRUCTURE - WHO SEQUENCES THE WRITE, read out of pg_trigger and pg_proc rather than guessed: a page writing two tables through two awaited client calls has NO transaction around them, so a 500, a closed laptop or a dead network between them leaves the first applied and the second missing, and nothing errors afterwards. A page writing one table and letting a TRIGGER or an RPC write the second is atomic BY CONSTRUCTION, because one statement is one transaction. LEDGER - WHETHER A HALF-WRITE IS VISIBLE TODAY: 14 of 14 declared conservation invariants checked against live data and ALL HOLD. ★AND THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A LINK, which is what stops 'client-sequenced' from being a verdict about the tool: the control pair community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards is joined by the trigger handle_community_post_xp and the detector finds it. A detector that cannot see that link cannot see any link, and would report every page as client-sequenced. ★ROSTER: {"client-sequenced": 11, "single-or-no-write": 11}. FOR THIS PAGE THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT SATISFY THE ORACLE, so this is NOT green even though nothing is broken today. It writes alert_dismissals + amc_briefings; alert_dismissals + anomaly_signals; alert_dismissals + hive_audit_log and the database does NOT link them - no trigger, no single RPC writing both - so a failure between the two client calls leaves the first applied and the second missing, silently. Every declared invariant holds against live data, which is genuinely reassuring, but 'has not happened yet' is a statement about this dataset, not about the code; banking it green would convert an absence of evidence into a guarantee. ★RE-WALKED AFTER THIS SESSION'S TWELVE PRODUCT FIXES so the evidence carries digests of the code as it now stands - R4b expired the prior rows because the fixes changed the very functions they rested on. Re-WALKED, never re-baselined.

control.note: the trigger handle_community_post_xp writes the award ledger, so a detector that cannot see this link cannot see any link

evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - every declared ledger invariant holds against the live database, exercised transactionally rather than reasoned about. The exposure the gate reports rather than hides is the honest part: 11 pages sequence TWO writes client-side, which is structural risk (a tab closed between them leaves the second undone) and is recorded as exposure, not counted as a failure, because no half-write has actually occurred in the data. findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, which asks the oracle's question in the two halves it actually has.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, which asks the oracle's question in the two halves it actually has. STRUCTURE - WHO SEQUENCES THE WRITE, read out of pg_trigger and pg_proc rather than guessed. A page that writes two tables through two awaited client calls has NO transaction around them: a 500, a closed laptop or a dead network between the two leaves the first applied and the second missing, and nothing errors afterwards. A page that writes one table and lets a TRIGGER or an RPC write the second is atomic by construction, because one statement is one transaction. LEDGER - WHETHER A HALF-WRITE IS VISIBLE TODAY: 14 of 14 declared conservation invariants were checked against live data and ALL HOLD - the inventory running balance, transactions with no orphan item, every reply and every live safety post carrying its XP award row, no XP row outliving a deleted post unreversed, no staged reservation both consumed and released, one AMC briefing per hive per shift date, a scope item not completed twice, no project child outliving its project. ★AND THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A LINK, which is what stops 'client-sequenced' from being a verdict about the tool: the control pair community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards is joined by the trigger handle_community_post_xp, and the detector finds it. A detector that cannot see that link cannot see any link, and would report every page as client-sequenced. ROSTER-WIDE: 11 pages client-sequenced, 11 single-or-no-write. FOR THIS PAGE THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT SATISFY THE ORACLE, so this is NOT banked green even though nothing is broken today. The page writes alert_dismissals + amc_briefings; alert_dismissals + anomaly_signals; alert_dismissals + hive_audit_log and the database does NOT link them - no trigger, no single RPC that writes both. So the first clause of the oracle ('either lands whole or not at all') is false as a structural matter: a failure between the two client calls leaves the first applied and the second missing, silently. WHAT THE LEDGER SAYS IS THE OTHER HALF, and it is genuinely reassuring rather than decorative: every declared conservation invariant holds against live data, so no half-write has HAPPENED. But 'has not happened yet' is a statement about this dataset, not about the code - the same shape as a latent null-collapse that no row has triggered. Banking it green would convert an absence of evidence into a guarantee. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: either the second write moves behind a trigger or an RPC (making it atomic by construction, which is what 11 of the 22 pages already do and what the control pair demonstrates), or a probe interrupts the page BETWEEN the two calls and shows the ledger invariant catching the resulting half-state - which would prove the second clause with teeth instead of by absence. ★CORRECTION TO THE STRENGTH OF THIS CLAIM, made after reading what the pairs actually are. The prover enumerates every PAIR OF RELATIONS a page writes and asks whether the database links them - a cartesian over the page's write set, NOT a list of observed co-writes. Most of these pairs are therefore not one logical write split in two: community_posts + community_reactions are two separate user actions, asset_nodes + inventory_items are two different edits, and hive_audit_log pairs with everything because it is appended alongside many actions. A HALF-WRITE IS ONLY POSSIBLE WHERE A SINGLE ACTION WRITES BOTH TABLES, which is a smaller set than the pair count suggests - the plausible ones on this roster are flows where one submit genuinely lands two rows (resume_documents + resume_versions on an upload; logbook + schedule_items when a planned item is completed; asset_nodes + logbook when an asset is created during capture). Which pairs those are cannot be read from pg_trigger; it needs the page's write FUNCTIONS traced. SO THE ROW STAYS OWED FOR A NARROWER REASON THAN THE PAIR COUNT IMPLIES: the page writes multiple tables with no DB linkage, which MAY permit a half-write on whichever action writes two - and the ledger shows none has occurred. This is not a claim that every listed pair is a live risk, and the distinction is recorded rather than letting a large pair count read as a large defect. CONCRETE NEXT SLICE: not 'add triggers', but trace this page's write functions, identify which single actions write two tables, and interrupt only those between the calls.

findings.detail: FAILS: with 2 reads answered 500, this page renders **450 characters of text and says nothing about the failure** - no error sentence, no dash sentinel, no retry. This is the alert inbox, so a silent blank reads as 'nothing needs your attention' at the exact moment the system cannot tell whether anything does. A BLANK SURFACE IS NOT AN HONEST ANSWER. The oracle asks that a server fault be shown as a fault rather than as an empty result, and an empty screen is the most literal empty result there is: someone opening this page during a backend fault cannot tell it from a page with nothing in it. THREE PAGES IN THIS SAME SWEEP DO IT PROPERLY, so the instrument discriminates and the pattern exists in-repo: hive says 'Could not reach your hive. Check your connection and refresh the page, or rejoin using your invite code.'; inventory says 'Could not load your inventory - Stock levels are unknown right now, not zero.'; pm-scheduler says 'Could not load PM compliance - Overdue PMs are unknown right now, not zero.' Each names the domain consequence rather than the HTTP status. TO FINISH: render the failure verdict and dash the tiles on the error path, in the shape those three pages already use. MEASURED BY FAILING EVERY READ AT window.fetch AND COUNTING WHAT THE PAGE DOES NEXT. Each `/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/` request is answered with a synthetic 500 (`{"code":"500"}`, Content-Type application/json) while `/auth/v1/` is left untouched so the session survives - so the page sees a server fault, not a dead network, and supabase-js resolves it into an error object exactly as PostgREST would. Interceptions are counted and a verdict over zero failed reads is refused as vacuous. THE INJECTION HAD TO MOVE FROM THE TRANSPORT TO window.fetch, AND THAT MATTERS FOR TRUST. An earlier pass used Playwright's `route()` and intercepted **0** requests on all 8 pages while they rendered real data - a registered service worker sits between the page and the transport in a warm context, so route() never saw the calls. Every verdict from that pass would have been false, and the interception counter is the only reason it was caught rather than banked. AND THE READING IS GUARDED INSIDE THE EVALUATE: it refuses unless the auth token holds the expected uid, `location.pathname` still ends in this page's own file, and the body is NOT in the 13,000-16,000 char landing-page band. A previous unguarded pass returned byte-identical output for seven different pages - 14,677 chars of marketing copy - because the session had expired and every page had redirected to `index.html?signin=1`. Seven page-specific verdicts, all of them the landing page. The guard is not ceremony.

findings.title: RETRACTED - the fail_timeout failure I recorded here was MY main-scoped text read missing a body-level notice, not a defect on this page
findings.detail: RETRACTED - THIS WAS MY INSTRUMENT, NOT THIS PAGE. I recorded fail_timeout failing on 11 of 16 pages and fail_partial on 13 of 16, described them as pages that say nothing on a timeout and present a partial result as complete, and wrote per-page findings saying so. All four CC oracles now pass on 12 of 12 pages, and NOTHING was changed on any timeout or partial code path in between. What changed is the PROBE: its text scope was document.querySelector('main'), and these pages render their failure messages into toasts, banners and live regions - which are fixed-position and therefore direct children of <body>, because a fixed element inside a transformed or overflow-clipped ancestor positions against that ancestor instead of the viewport. main.innerText could never contain them. So the pages were speaking and the probe was deaf. HOW I FOUND IT, and why it is worth recording rather than quietly re-banking: I added a central 401 notice at getDb()'s transport seam, VERIFIED it rendering - the element was in the DOM carrying the text - and fail_401 still read every sub-assertion false. That contradiction is what exposed the scope bug. The failure oracle now reads main PLUS live/alert/notice containers, deduped, and deliberately NOT all of body, because nav and hub chrome carry standing words like 'offline' and 'retry' that would forge a pass on every page. WHAT SURVIVES: the fail_401 finding was REAL. Before the central fix there was no session notice on any page at all - no element existed to be missed - so 12 of 12 pages genuinely told a reader nothing when their session died, and the fix at getDb() is what created the notice they now show. That one is not withdrawn. Only the timeout and partial claims are, and they are withdrawn in full. THE LESSON IS THE ONE THIS ARC KEEPS RE-LEARNING: an instrument that measures the wrong REGION produces well-formed readings, and a uniform failure across many pages should raise suspicion of the probe before it is written up as a platform defect. The same lens-scope error once measured 15 of 518 nodes for contrast because it scoped to <main> while the report mounted outside it.

findings.title: RETRACTION SUPERSEDED - the withdrawal above rested on a contaminated reading; fail_partial genuinely FAILS here (9 of 12 pages), reinstated
findings.detail: THE RETRACTION ON THIS ROW WAS ITSELF WRONG, and this note supersedes it. Three measurements of fail_partial exist and only the middle one is contaminated: (1) FIRST READ, text scope = <main>: failed on 13 of 16 pages. (2) SECOND READ, after I widened the scope to include body-level notice regions: passed on 12 of 12 - and on the strength of that I retracted the finding on 12 pages, writing that 'the pages were speaking and the probe was deaf'. (3) THIRD READ, after I made my own 401 notice CLEAR ITSELF: fails on 9 of 12. NOTHING ON ANY PARTIAL CODE PATH CHANGED ACROSS THOSE THREE. What changed in (2) is that the central session notice I had just added to getDb() was still pinned to the page from the 401 injection earlier in the same failures() run, so namesTheFailure was matching MY OWN leftover text - 'Your session expired, so this page could not be loaded' - rather than anything the page said about a truncated payload. Reading (1) and reading (3) AGREE with each other; (2) is the outlier, and (2) is the one I acted on. SO THE ORIGINAL FINDING STANDS, at 9 of 12 rather than 13 of 16: on this page a truncated payload is rendered without the reader being told part of the data is missing. The withdrawal note above should be read as evidence about my instrument's history, not as an exoneration of this page. WHY THIS HAPPENED, because the mechanism matters more than the count: I fixed one artefact (a main-scoped text read) and in the same window introduced another (a notice that outlived its injection), then used a measurement taken between the two to overturn a finding. A correction is only as good as the reading behind it, and a reading taken while another fix is half-landed is not a baseline. The rule I keep re-deriving: change ONE thing, re-measure, and never let a retraction rest on a single run - especially not one that flips a uniform FAIL into a uniform PASS, which is the same too-good-to-be-true signature that should raise suspicion of the instrument in either direction.

findings.detail: A PARTIAL READ RENDERS AS A COMPLETE, SELF-CONSISTENT COUNT - the denominator moved with the numerator, which is exactly what makes it invisible. Healthy: 52 alerts of 60. With a 500 injected into v_alert_truth / alert_dismissals / v_anomaly_truth (2 interceptions, non-vacuous), the page shows '32 of 40 alerts need eyes now' and renders 32 alerts in full detail, each with its asset, its age and its action links. Nothing on the surface is malformed, empty or flagged: 20 alerts simply ceased to exist, and the ratio still reads plausibly because 52/60 became 32/40 rather than 32/60. WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN A TOTAL FAILURE: a blank page is obviously broken, and this is not. It is a confident, detailed, fully populated inbox that is missing a third of the plant's alerts, including - on the healthy read - PMs 12 to 19 days overdue and parts below reorder point. The oracle's own words are 'a truncated payload keeps what arrived AND names the failure, so a partial result is not presented as a complete one': what arrived was kept, and the failure was never named. SAME SHAPE AS the four-exclusions-shrank-the-denominator lesson - a metric stays believable precisely because both halves shrank together, so neither a ratio check nor an eyeball can catch it. A count that can be partial must carry the total it EXPECTED, or state that it could not establish one. || METHOD: MEASURED AS A TIMELINE, NOT A SNAPSHOT, and that is the whole point of the reading. A 500 is injected into the page's own reads (fetch wrapped before load; /auth/v1/ deliberately NOT blocked so the identity guard can still read a valid session), the interception is COUNTED and a verdict over zero interceptions is refused as vacuous, and then the surface is sampled five times across ~15s rather than once. WHY THE TIMELINE MATTERS: a single-instant reading of this oracle is not reproducible, and this bank holds the receipts in both directions. An earlier pass recorded 'says nothing on failure' across 11 of 16 pages and then RETRACTED it, because that lens was <main>-scoped and missed a body-level notice; a later pass recorded all four CC oracles passing on 12 of 12. Sampling over time shows BOTH WERE TRUE AT DIFFERENT INSTANTS - the failure notice is a toast that auto-dismisses while the zeros it was explaining stay on screen indefinitely. So 'did the page speak?' is the wrong question, and 'is the reader who arrives three seconds late still told?' is the right one. POSITIVE CONTROL in the same run: the identical lens caught pm-scheduler's notice at all five samples, so a silent reading is the page's silence and not the lens's blindness - which is the check the retracted finding lacked.

A 'number-bearing element' is defined narrowly: a LEAF element whose entire trimmed text is numeric after stripping currency, separators, % and a unit suffix - '9' and '61%' qualify, '9 open items carried over' does not because it labels itself. A label counts when it is non-numeric text of >=3 chars in the element's own aria-label/title or in an ancestor's text with the number removed, climbing at most 4 ancestors and only while that ancestor's subtree is section-sized or smaller (<=400 chars) - both bounds are load-bearing, because too tight invents defects (it once called analytics' fully-documented OEE hero unlabelled for being 35 chars too verbose) and too loose makes the pass free by accepting a whole section's prose as a label. TWO ORACLES, ONE TRUTH CONDITION - stated because it would be dishonest to present this as an independent second measurement. This bank's CM oracle `what_is_this_number` ('a person can state what the number means from the surface alone') is already green from this SAME instrument and this SAME reading; CE's `number_explained` asks 'a person can say what the number MEANS without leaving the surface'. That two of the 200 slots ask one question is a FRAME observation, and it belongs to the roadmap's synthesis rather than to this row. SCOPE, precisely: this is V1 only. The prover walks the view each page OPENS ON, so the V2 row's second view (a modal, a sheet, a tab) is NOT covered by this reading and stays owed.

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_source_chip.mjs, live: 41 views graded across the roster - 18 make a TRUE provenance claim, 23 make NO claim, 0 name a feed they never read.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_source_chip.mjs, live: 41 views graded across the roster - 18 make a TRUE provenance claim, 23 make NO claim, 0 name a feed they never read. THE ORACLE MATTERS MORE THAN MOST UI TEXT: a source chip is a promise that a number came from named feeds, and a reader uses it to decide whether to trust the figure. A chip naming a feed the page never queried is worse than no chip, because it manufactures confidence. SO THE CLAIM IS CHECKED AGAINST THE NETWORK, not the source: every PostgREST /rest/v1/<relation> the view actually requests is captured at runtime, and each schema-shaped token the chip names must correspond to one. It is deliberately ONE-DIRECTIONAL - a chip that SUMMARISES is fine, a chip that INVENTS is not. ★TWO MANUFACTURED FINDINGS WERE CAUGHT AND REMOVED BEFORE ANY OF THIS WAS BANKED. The first version of the token test counted the bare word `logbook`, so asset-hub and analytics were both reported as naming an unread feed - on the strength of ordinary prose: 'Based on your asset records, risk scores, logbook, failure analysis'. That is a sentence describing FEATURES to a person, not an assertion about a table, and analytics is right on its own terms - it reads analytics_snapshots, a snapshot DERIVED from logbook data, which is precisely what 'saved snapshot ... based on your logbook' says. A keyword match over human prose is how a page's own helper text becomes a defect. The test now counts a token only when it is unmistakably schema-shaped (a v_ prefix, a _truth suffix, or a known table prefix + underscore); bare English words never qualify. ★AND THE VIEW IS READ INSIDE ITSELF. V1 is graded at page scope and V2 inside the OPENED view via the shared tools/dialog_targets.mjs registry, because crediting a V2 row with a V1 reading is the one-measurement-swept-two-views error this bank has already paid for once. NOT BANKED GREEN: this view displays NO source chip at all (0 on screen while the surface requested 14 relation(s)). A surface that makes no provenance claim has not made a TRUE one, and the oracle asks whether the claim is true - so silence cannot satisfy it. Scoring it green would credit the absence of a promise as a kept promise. THIS IS ALSO NOT AUTOMATICALLY A DEFECT. Most of the 23 are V2 dialogs - a composer, a confirm sheet, a detail panel - which display a form rather than a derived figure, and a provenance chip on a surface that states no number would be noise. WHAT SETTLES IT is the per-view question the bank actually asks: does THIS view show a figure a reader would want provenance for? If yes, the chip is missing and this is a real finding; if no, the row is declared-na under R10 with 'this view states no derived figure' as the reason and the CM comprehension oracles as its replacement. Left owed rather than guessed, because that question is per-view and answering it from a count would be inventing the verdict.

findings.title: NOT MEASURED - AND THE HONEST REASON IS THAT MY PROBE MEASURED ITSELF.
findings.detail: NOT MEASURED - AND THE HONEST REASON IS THAT MY PROBE MEASURED ITSELF. The dismissal write is proven (alert_dismissals 0 -> 1, cleaned back to 0), but the VISIBLE half was not graded: the probe captured the label of the element it clicked - '⏳ Snooze 7d', the BUTTON'S OWN TEXT - rather than the alert it belonged to, and its row selector ([class*="alert-row"],[data-dedupe]) matched ZERO elements before or after. So the 'still there' answer it produced was about a button, not about an alert, and it is worth nothing. ★THE REAL DIFFICULTY IS POLARITY, not selectors. Every other page in this family proves a row APPEARED; this one must prove a row DISAPPEARED - and a disappearance is far easier to fake, because a page that failed to render at all also shows nothing. A removal check therefore needs a BEFORE state that is known to be present: capture the specific alert's identity while it is on screen, confirm it renders, dismiss it, then confirm THAT identity is gone while the rest of the feed still renders. Without the last clause, a blank page passes. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: read the feed's real row selector from the page's own render (the dedupeKey is 'risk:'/'stock:'/'pm:'/'pattern:'/'staging:' + a name, so the row carries a stable identity), assert that identity present, dismiss, and assert it absent WITH a non-empty feed as the control.

Every other page in this family proves something APPEARED; a prover that only knows that shape cannot grade this one. ★A DISAPPEARANCE IS FAR EASIER TO FAKE THAN AN APPEARANCE, which is why this check has three clauses and not one: a page that failed to render at all also shows nothing, so 'absent' on its own is worthless.   1. PRESENT BEFORE - the specific alert '3x repeat failure on CR-001' was confirmed RENDERED by geometry (real box, display/visibility/opacity) before anything was clicked. Its identity was taken from the ROW's own longest text line, deliberately excluding the button's label - my first attempt captured the button's text ('Snooze 7d') and produced an answer about a button rather than an alert.   2. ABSENT AFTER - the same identity is no longer rendered once dismissed.   3. NON-EMPTY CONTROL - the rest of the feed still renders (4,682 -> 5,118 characters). Without this clause a blank page passes the oracle, which is the empty-denominator failure this bank exists to catch, inverted. AND THE WRITE IS PROVEN ALONGSIDE IT: alert_dismissals went 0 -> 1 for this hive, read with psql as postgres, then cleaned back to the measured baseline of 0 - verified by re-count, not assumed. ★WHY THIS SURFACE DESERVES THE RIGOUR: the file records that a dismissal fired at a dead network once died silently, 'and a supervisor believed a plant alert had been handled'. An inbox that forgets a dismissal is annoying; one that ACCEPTS a dismissal that never landed is dangerous. The oracle here is not decoration - it is the difference between an alert being handled and only looking handled.

findings.title: NOT BANKED, AND THE REASON IS A REFUSAL TO RE-IMPLEMENT THE PAGE IN SQL.
findings.detail: NOT BANKED, AND THE REASON IS A REFUSAL TO RE-IMPLEMENT THE PAGE IN SQL. #ah-critical-hero shows 51 and is labelled 'High-severity alerts' (data-rag-tile=alert-hub:high_severity_alerts). It is NOT a single query: alert-hub fans out five reads in one Promise.allSettled - v_risk_truth, inventory_items_truth, pm_assets, the automation/pattern log and parts staging - and the hero is the COMPOSITE of high-severity items across all five, each with its own severity derivation (inventory maps qty<=0 to 'critical' and qty<=reorder/2 to 'high'; staging derives from risk_score >= 0.85 when no canonical level exists). ★AND THE FIRST SOURCE IS CAPPED AT 20 ROWS (.limit(20) on v_risk_truth), so even that component is not a count - it is a page of one. Writing SQL to reproduce all five derivations would be building a second implementation of the page's own severity logic and then reporting the two implementations' disagreements as product defects. That is the failure this bank exists to prevent, and it is worse here than elsewhere because the surface is a SAFETY inbox. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT, in the shape that already worked for pm-scheduler's client-side rollup: not an equality against one query, but a PARTITION or a BOUND that is true regardless of the derivations - e.g. the hero must not exceed the total number of alert-bearing objects the five sources can produce, and every alert the list renders must appear in exactly one severity bucket. That needs the five source counts enumerated per-source rather than guessed, which is the next concrete slice for this row. FOR REFERENCE, ONE COMPONENT MEASURED CLEANLY: v_risk_truth holds the critical+high rows for this hive, which is the number the .limit(20) read is paging through - recorded so the next walk starts from a measured component rather than from scratch.

observed.why_not_settled: the hero is a composite across five reads with per-source severity derivations; one of them is .limit(20)-capped
observed.refusal: reproducing five derivations in SQL would be a second implementation whose disagreements would be reported as defects
observed.to_settle: a partition/bound like pm-scheduler's, built from per-source counts rather than a single equality

findings.detail: NOT PROVEN - NO SUBJECT EXISTS TO ACT ON, AND THAT IS A FIXTURE GAP RATHER THAN A PAGE DEFECT. This view's person-caused write is acknowledging an anomaly (anomaly_signals.update, driven from a [data-anomaly-id] control). The table holds ZERO rows, so there is nothing to acknowledge and no control is rendered. ★THE SEED PATH WAS ATTEMPTED PROPERLY BEFORE CALLING IT A GAP. compute_anomaly_signals(p_hive_id) refuses a direct psql call - 'not authorized for hive ...' - which is CORRECT security behaviour and worth recording as a positive: the RPC checks membership rather than trusting its caller. So it was driven the legitimate way instead, by loading the page SIGNED IN as the supervisor, which is exactly when the page calls it. anomaly_signals remained at 0 and zero acknowledge controls rendered. ★SO THE DETECTOR RAN AND FOUND NOTHING ANOMALOUS IN THE CURRENT DATA - a legitimate state, not a failure. Asserting a defect here would be asserting one in the absence of the thing the assertion is about, which is the empty-denominator error this bank exists to catch: 'no acknowledge control rendered' and 'the acknowledge control is broken' are opposite findings that look identical from a page with no anomalies. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: seed sensor or risk data that genuinely trips compute_anomaly_signals, then acknowledge the resulting signal and assert the row updates AND the surface reflects it. The platform has seeders for this class of gap; missing data is a thing to regenerate, never a ceiling. NOTHING WAS WRITTEN: anomaly_signals was 0 before and 0 after.

findings.title: MEASURED AND FAILING - 3 of 3 user-triggered write(s) on this page fire with NO connectivity check before them: actOnAmcBrief (listener-bound), dismissAlert, acknowledgeAlert.
findings.detail: MEASURED AND FAILING - 3 of 3 user-triggered write(s) on this page fire with NO connectivity check before them: actOnAmcBrief (listener-bound), dismissAlert, acknowledgeAlert. THE PREMISE WAS CHECKED FIRST, because filing this against a page that is guarded elsewhere would be a manufactured finding: utils.js already defines whRequireOnline(action, notify) and exposes it as window.whRequireOnline, and it already carries the exact sentence this oracle asks for - 'You are offline. <action> needs a connection - nothing was sent, so nothing is half-done.' The scanner's GUARD pattern matches RequireOnline( and navigator.onLine === false, so a page that called either would have counted as guarded. None of these writes call anything. This is NON-ADOPTION of a centralized, correctly-worded helper, not a missing message. WHY THE PLATFORM'S EXISTING GREEN DOES NOT COVER THIS: tools/validate_offline_write_guard.py PASSES at fail-severity, but its PAGES list is exactly ['marketplace.html', 'marketplace-seller.html'] - 19 writes on two pages. None of the 22 roster pages is in its scope, so its green says nothing about them. And widening that list alone would NOT be enough: the validator's user_invokable() recognises only window.X = and inline onclick/onchange/onsubmit, so of the 53 exposed writes measured across the roster it would see 37 and miss the 16 bound with addEventListener. WHAT A PASSIVE BANNER DOES NOT DO, since every page already adopts one: the banner states the condition, it does not refuse the action. The button still fires, the request still leaves, and the person still cannot tell whether their work landed - which is the whole distinction this oracle draws. THE FIX IS ONE LINE PER WRITE at the top of each function - if (!whRequireOnline('<gerund>', showToast)) return; - and the highest-stakes ones on this page should go first. WHAT THE NEXT WALK NEEDS after the guards land: prove it LIVE rather than statically, and note that setOffline does not flip navigator.onLine in the page, so the probe must override navigator.onLine AND block the network, then assert that zero requests fired and the sentence reached the person.

findings.detail: FAILS: with 2 reads answered 500, **this page offers no retry control at all** - zero visible elements whose label or handler mentions retry or try-again. It also says nothing at all about the failure (450 visible characters) - on the surface whose whole purpose is telling someone what needs attention. SO A READER'S ONLY RECOURSE IS A FULL PAGE RELOAD, which on a phone in a plant means losing whatever was on screen and paying the whole load again on the connection that just failed. THE PLATFORM HAS THE PATTERN ALREADY, so this is unadopted rather than undesigned: community renders a toast reading 'Couldn't load the community feed. Check your connection and try again.' with a **Retry** button beside it, and public-feed's Retry was measured firing a real re-request and then rendering 15 posts. Six of the seven pages measured in this sweep have neither. WHAT WOULD PASS IT: a control that re-issues the failed read and is measurable as such - the probe counts requests fired after the click, so a button that merely re-renders the previous failure fails too. That distinction is not hypothetical: it is the exact defect commit 3ddef99d fixed on public-feed. MEASURED BY FAILING EVERY READ AT window.fetch AND COUNTING WHAT THE PAGE DOES NEXT. Each `/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/` request is answered with a synthetic 500 (`{"code":"500"}`, Content-Type application/json) while `/auth/v1/` is left untouched so the session survives - so the page sees a server fault, not a dead network, and supabase-js resolves it into an error object exactly as PostgREST would. Interceptions are counted and a verdict over zero failed reads is refused as vacuous. THE INJECTION HAD TO MOVE FROM THE TRANSPORT TO window.fetch, AND THAT MATTERS FOR TRUST. An earlier pass used Playwright's `route()` and intercepted **0** requests on all 8 pages while they rendered real data - a registered service worker sits between the page and the transport in a warm context, so route() never saw the calls. Every verdict from that pass would have been false, and the interception counter is the only reason it was caught rather than banked. AND THE READING IS GUARDED INSIDE THE EVALUATE: it refuses unless the auth token holds the expected uid, `location.pathname` still ends in this page's own file, and the body is NOT in the 13,000-16,000 char landing-page band. A previous unguarded pass returned byte-identical output for seven different pages - 14,677 chars of marketing copy - because the session had expired and every page had redirected to `index.html?signin=1`. Seven page-specific verdicts, all of them the landing page. The guard is not ceremony.

MEASURED with live-state-runner.js::availability({settle:1500}) driven across the whole product roster by tools/prove_availability_pages.mjs - the SAME lens tools/walk_owed_scenarios.mjs uses for the marketplace surfaces, so the two banks cannot disagree about what these words mean. ★THE INDUCTION IS PROVEN TO HAVE LANDED, which is the difference between a verdict and a guess: the lens reports inductionLanded, the number of reads that actually went out under the injected condition, and refuses to score a page that never re-queried. Its own comment records why - it once read retry_path:false / fallback:silentlyStale on a surface that handles both correctly, because closure-scoped loaders meant the page never moved, and it scored the UNCHANGED page. Every verdict banked here carries inductionLanded > 0 and inconclusive:false. ★AND THE LENS IS PROVEN ABLE TO PASS, so a FAIL is not a blanket instrument failure: across the roster it returned retry_path 3 PASS / 19 FAIL, rate_limit_legible 1/21, fallback_engaged 7/15, slow_honest 10/12. public-feed passes all four - consistent with its own history, since it is the page fixed so a failed read renders an error rather than 'No public posts yet'. RETRY PATH - FAILS, and the half that is certain is the half that matters. Under an injected 500 this page offers ZERO retry affordances: no 'try again', no 'reload', no 'refresh' control. That is confirmed TWO independent ways - the lens counted affordances:0, and a separate direct probe that 500'd every /rest/v1/ request and scanned the whole document for a retry control also found none. A person whose data failed to load has nothing to press. ★ONE HALF OF THIS VERDICT IS INSTRUMENT-DEPENDENT AND IS RECORDED AS SUCH RATHER THAN BANKED AS FACT: the lens also reported saysFailure:False. My direct probe, which failed EVERY read rather than the subset the lens induces, and which scanned the whole page rather than <main>, found that this page DOES say something failed under a total outage. So the page's failure MESSAGING may be better than the lens's number suggests - a partial induction can leave a surface half-populated and quiet. The missing retry CONTROL is not in doubt; the missing failure SENTENCE is, on this page. WHY IT IS NOT BANKED GREEN ANYWAY: the oracle asks for a retry PATH, and a failure a person cannot act on is the shape this family exists to catch - 'a failure that offers a retry which does not re-attempt is worse than one that offers none', and offering none at all is the floor of that same scale.

★RETRACTED CONTEXT ON THIS ROW'S RECORDED TALLY: it lists rate_limit_legible as 1P/21F. That figure is true of THIS LENS and misleading about the platform, and is retracted as evidence of any gap. 42 rate_limit_legible rows are banked green on a 2026-08-09 induction against the REAL limit - 400 logbook inserts inside BEGIN...ROLLBACK as an authenticated member, refused with 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' plus HINT logbook_daily_user, and a second hive-tier quota at SQLSTATE 54000 that states its remedy. THE PLATFORM'S RATE LIMITING IS LEGIBLE. This lens asked a different question - whether a page's TEXT names a limit under a FAKE 429 injected at the fetch layer, a client-rendering question about a condition the server never produced. PRECEDENCE (roadmap 6l/6m): a prover that induced the REAL condition outranks a lens that simulated one; the disagreement is scope, never regression. THE VERDICT ON THIS ROW'S OWN KEY IS UNAFFECTED - it rests on its own induction, which landed (inductionLanded > 0).

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_retry_path.mjs (new) - EVERY /rest/v1/ read failed with a 500, then the network released and the retry pressed.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_retry_path.mjs (new) - EVERY /rest/v1/ read failed with a 500, then the network released and the retry pressed. ★THE INDUCTION IS TOTAL, NOT PARTIAL, AND THAT CHANGED THE ANSWER. The availability lens fails a SUBSET of reads and reported 'affordances: 0' for pages that demonstrably DO render a Retry on other paths. Failing every request is what actually reaches a page's error branch. ★AND BOTH CLAUSES ARE MEASURED, because the second is the one that ships broken: a retry must RE-ATTEMPT and the failure must CLEAR. hive proved why - its first fix sent 3 fresh reads and left the page byte-for-byte unchanged, because it re-rendered from a cache still holding the failed state. A retry that re-attempts and does not recover is worse than none: it invites pressing again. ★THE ROSTER, so no page's verdict rests on its own reading alone: PASS 6 (hive, logbook, inventory, skillmatrix, public-feed, resume) | NO-RETRY 9 | NO-RECOVER 3 | NO-ATTEMPT 1 | SILENT 3. ★THE COMPONENT ALREADY EXISTS - THIS IS ADOPTION, NOT DESIGN. whListError(el, message, onRetry) in utils.js renders the inline error WITH a working Retry, and 16 pages already import it. Six pages passing is what separates 'nobody built this' from 'not every read path routes through it'. FOR THIS PAGE: it SAYS a failure happened and offers NOTHING TO PRESS. Telling someone to check their connection is advice; a control they can press is a path, and the oracle asks for the second. The fix is to route this read's error branch through whListError, which this roster already uses on six pages - a per-path edit, not a design decision.

findings.title: The DB's legible rate-limit message is likely MASKED by a generic client string on the write path
findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

evidence.asserts: when a limit is hit the refusal is legible - it names the limit, the scope, and when it clears, and carries a machine-readable key so a client can tell WHICH limit fired
evidence.checked: FIRED FOR REAL, NOT READ FROM THE SOURCE - and then the source was read to confirm the second tier. Inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK as an authenticated member (role SET, not just claims), a burst of 400 logbook inserts was attempted. The trigger refused with: **'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.'** carrying HINT 'logbook_daily_user'. Verified clean afterwards: 0 probe rows survived the rollback. WHY THIS COUNTS AS LEGIBLE, CLAUSE BY CLAUSE: it names the LIMIT (100), names WHAT was hit (today's free limit, i.e. a per-user daily cap rather than a system fault), tells the reader WHEN IT CLEARS ('Resets at midnight') so they know whether to wait or escalate, and ships a machine-readable HINT key ('logbook_daily_user') so a client can branch on WHICH limit fired instead of pattern-matching English. That combination - human sentence plus stable key - is what separates a legible limit from 'permission denied'. THERE IS A SECOND TIER AND IT IS ALSO LEGIBLE: check_hive_quota_logbook raises 'logbook cumulative quota exceeded for hive % (% >= %)' with ERRCODE 54000 and a HINT that old records can be archived - so the per-user daily cap and the per-hive cumulative quota are distinguishable by SQLSTATE and by message, and the hive-level one tells the reader the remedy (archive) rather than just the fact. ANCHORED ON supabase/migrations PER A13 - the message lives in the trigger body.
evidence.value_checked: 400-insert burst -> 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' HINT logbook_daily_user; hive tier raises 54000 'cumulative quota exceeded' + archive hint; 0 probe rows survived rollback

findings.title: FAILS BOTH CLAUSES. The oracle: 'when the primary is down the fallback engages and the surface says which it used, rather than pretending nothing happened.' findings.detail: FAILS BOTH CLAUSES. The oracle: 'when the primary is down the fallback engages and the surface says which it used, rather than pretending nothing happened.' Two clauses, and this page is measured against both. MEASURED with 2 reads answered 500 under the guarded probe: the page renders **450 characters and says nothing whatsoever about the failure** - no fallback, no error sentence, no dash sentinel, no retry control. This is the alert inbox, so silence reads as 'nothing needs your attention' at the moment the system cannot tell whether anything does. PRETENDING NOTHING HAPPENED IS EXACTLY WHAT A SILENT SURFACE DOES. The reader cannot distinguish a backend fault from a genuinely empty plant, and the page offers no way to find out. THE SWEEP DISCRIMINATES, so this is the page and not the probe: hive answers the same injection with 'Could not reach your hive. Check your connection and refresh the page, or rejoin using your invite code.', inventory with 'Stock levels are unknown right now, not zero', pm-scheduler with 'Overdue PMs are unknown right now, not zero.' THERE IS NO READ FALLBACK ON THIS PLATFORM, AND THAT IS PROVEN FROM THE SERVICE WORKER'S SOURCE RATHER THAN INFERRED. `sw.js` handles API traffic in one branch - `if (url.includes('supabase.co') || url.includes('fonts.goog') ...) e.respondWith(fetch(e.request).catch(() => new Response('', { status: 503 })))` (sw.js:195-200) - so a failed read resolves to an EMPTY 503 body. And `cache.put` appears **nowhere in the file**, so no API response is ever stored: `caches.match()` cannot hit for a `/rest/v1/` URL because nothing put one there. The 26-entry `SHELL_FILES` precache holds HTML, CSS and JS only. SO THE FIRST CLAUSE CANNOT BE SATISFIED FOR READS BY CONSTRUCTION - there is nothing to engage. The offline layer this platform does have is for WRITES (the `wh_logbook_offline` / `wh_dayplanner_offline` / `wh_assethub_offline` IndexedDB queues), which is a different oracle. That makes the second clause the whole test: does the surface say the primary is down, or does it pretend nothing happened? MEASURED TWO INDEPENDENT WAYS, so the reading does not rest on one injection style. (1) Every `/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/` request answered with a synthetic 500 at `window.fetch`, `/auth/v1/` left alone so the session survives, interceptions counted and a zero-interception run refused as vacuous. (2) A genuine `setOffline(true)` navigation with the service-worker cache WARM. THE SECOND METHOD TOOK THREE ATTEMPTS TO GET HONEST, WHICH IS WHY IT IS TRUSTWORTHY NOW. Navigating to `/workhive/logbook.html` offline served the branded offline shell every time - not because the page is unavailable offline, but because `SHELL_FILES` precaches ROOT paths (`/logbook.html`) and the `/workhive/` prefix is a different cache key. Measured at the path the cache actually holds, the real page is served. A verdict from the prefixed path would have described a cache miss and called it product behaviour. AND ONE LIMIT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN PAPERED OVER: under Playwright's `setOffline(true)`, `navigator.onLine` still read **true** and `wh-conn-chip` still read 'Online' (hidden). The app's own offline DETECTION therefore never fired, so this reading covers 'the primary is down' but NOT 'the app knows it is offline'. The absence of an offline banner is consequently NOT charged against the page here. A probe that wants that claim must also override `navigator.onLine` and dispatch the `offline` event.

findings.title: GUARDED AND OWED ON A CLOCK, not on a missing guard.
findings.detail: GUARDED AND OWED ON A CLOCK, not on a missing guard. actOnAmcBrief was guarded this session with whRequireOnline, placed BEFORE the reject confirmation on purpose: making a supervisor confirm 'the crew will not act on it' and only then failing is worse than refusing up front, because the decision has already been made and they cannot tell whether it was recorded. The message goes to showAmcMsg, this card's own channel, where 'Supervisor approval required.' also lands. This is unambiguously the online-only class - an approval whose write carries an optimistic lock (.eq('id',..).eq('hive_id',..).eq('status','pending')), and a lock that never reaches the database protects nothing. WHY IT CANNOT BE WALKED YET, measured with explicit ::text casts because reading a shifted date is what produced two earlier false diagnoses on this page: UTC 2026-08-17 20:04 / Manila 2026-08-18 04:04 / Manila-today 2026-08-18, and amc_briefings holds 2026-08-17=pending, 2026-08-14=expired, 2026-08-13=expired, 2026-08-08=expired. There is no brief for Manila-today because it is 04:04 and the generator runs around 06:00 Manila. The card is correctly hidden, so the approve/reject pair does not exist to press. AND I DID NOT FORCE IT: seeding a row for 2026-08-18 would succeed (the unique constraint only blocks a duplicate DATE) but would fabricate plant-risk content in a shared database, and triggering the real analytics-orchestrator generation is a PAID AI call. Waiting for the scheduled generation costs nothing. WHAT THE NEXT WALK NEEDS: run between 06:00 and 24:00 Manila, then press Approve offline and assert zero amc_briefings requests plus the sentence in showAmcMsg. The stranded-brief defect this view also carries (a pending brief becomes unapprovable after the Manila day rolls over, because actOnAmcBrief binds to today's _amcBrief and the historic feed offers actionLabel: '') is recorded on this view's CO-ux-recovery rows, not here.

observed.write_class: approval - online-only; its write carries an optimistic lock on status='pending'
observed.why_unwalkable: no brief for Manila-today (04:04; generator runs ~06:00 Manila) so the card is correctly hidden
observed.not_forced_because: seeding fabricates plant-risk content; real generation is a PAID AI call
observed.next_walk: 06:00-24:00 Manila, press Approve offline, assert 0 amc_briefings requests + the showAmcMsg sentence

No page error was raised in any case. Re-walked against the post-fix tree

MEASURED with live-state-runner.js::availability({settle:1500}) driven across the whole product roster by tools/prove_availability_pages.mjs - the SAME lens tools/walk_owed_scenarios.mjs uses for the marketplace surfaces, so the two banks cannot disagree about what these words mean. ★THE INDUCTION IS PROVEN TO HAVE LANDED, which is the difference between a verdict and a guess: the lens reports inductionLanded, the number of reads that actually went out under the injected condition, and refuses to score a page that never re-queried. Its own comment records why - it once read retry_path:false / fallback:silentlyStale on a surface that handles both correctly, because closure-scoped loaders meant the page never moved, and it scored the UNCHANGED page. Every verdict banked here carries inductionLanded > 0 and inconclusive:false. ★AND THE LENS IS PROVEN ABLE TO PASS, so a FAIL is not a blanket instrument failure: across the roster it returned retry_path 3 PASS / 19 FAIL, rate_limit_legible 1/21, fallback_engaged 7/15, slow_honest 10/12. public-feed passes all four - consistent with its own history, since it is the page fixed so a failed read renders an error rather than 'No public posts yet'. FALLBACK ENGAGED - FAILS. under failure the page neither engaged a visible fallback nor said it was showing saved data. Detail: {"primaryDown": true, "rowsWithPrimaryDown": 9, "chromeFloorMeasuredEmpty": 9, "domainRowsSurviving": 0, "saysFailure": false, "labelsProvenance": false}.

★RETRACTED CONTEXT ON THIS ROW'S RECORDED TALLY: it lists rate_limit_legible as 1P/21F. That figure is true of THIS LENS and misleading about the platform, and is retracted as evidence of any gap. 42 rate_limit_legible rows are banked green on a 2026-08-09 induction against the REAL limit - 400 logbook inserts inside BEGIN...ROLLBACK as an authenticated member, refused with 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' plus HINT logbook_daily_user, and a second hive-tier quota at SQLSTATE 54000 that states its remedy. THE PLATFORM'S RATE LIMITING IS LEGIBLE. This lens asked a different question - whether a page's TEXT names a limit under a FAKE 429 injected at the fetch layer, a client-rendering question about a condition the server never produced. PRECEDENCE (roadmap 6l/6m): a prover that induced the REAL condition outranks a lens that simulated one; the disagreement is scope, never regression. THE VERDICT ON THIS ROW'S OWN KEY IS UNAFFECTED - it rests on its own induction, which landed (inductionLanded > 0).

scenarios.question: IDENTITY - authN from the JWT, authZ at the server, boundaries stated as boundaries and never rendered as emptiness
scenarios.oracle: another person's object id is refused, and the refusal is legible

evidence.asserts: another person's object id is refused, and the refusal is legible
evidence.checked: PASSES. WHICH OF THE GATE'S CHECKS PROVE THIS ORACLE (named, not inherited from 'the gate is green'): OBJECT-level access: the gate's cross-tenant READ and OWN-SCOPE WRITE checks - read_logbook_xhive and read_cxp_xhive (a FOREIGN hive's v_logbook_truth and community_xp return ZERO rows) and logbook_edit_ownscope (a member cannot UPDATE another hive's logbook entry). These are per-OBJECT refusals: the caller names a specific row they do not own and is refused, which is exactly what BOLA asks. Persona under test on this row: worker (tenant boundary) - and the gate's probe IS that persona, a real authenticated member of one hive reaching for another's data. WHAT WOULD HAVE FAILED IT: any one of those checks returning a row it should not, and the gate is known to fire because it was BUILT on real leaks it caught - 1,105 rows of a foreign tenant's logbook, a self-joinable membership, and a DELETE-then-reINSERT that un-banned a kicked worker. HOW IT WAS MEASURED, by REUSING the instrument the platform already owns instead of writing another: tools/validate_hive_isolation.py runs 26 invariants LIVE as a real authenticated member of one hive against a second, data-rich hive, every attempt inside a rolled-back transaction so the shared database is never polluted. Current result: 26 pass / 0 fail. IT IS ROLE-CORRECT, which is the only reason it means anything: it sets both the `authenticated` ROLE and the JWT claims. A probe carrying claims while still running as superuser bypasses RLS entirely and passes by construction - and that is not hypothetical, it cost a false finding on this very platform the same day, when an approved change order looked EDITABLE as `postgres` and is in fact refused for both a worker and a supervisor, because the guard deliberately exempts the admin path. IT IS RESEED-ROBUST: the actors and the foreign hive are resolved DYNAMICALLY from live hive_members rows rather than pinned as UUIDs, so a reseed cannot quietly turn the probe into a test of a dead hive - which would 403 for the WRONG reason and read as a pass. AND IT CARRIES NO-REGRESSION CHECKS (join_rpc_ok, founder_create_ok), so a gate that 'passed' by breaking the legitimate path would be caught rather than celebrated. WHY THIS ROW WAS STALE: it was hand-walked in an earlier session and banked with no `evidence.replay`, so nothing could re-earn it without a human repeating the whole probe. It now carries the command, which is the entire point of the A16 anti-stale discipline: 546 db-anchored rows on this platform are in exactly that position, and this is 176 of them coming out of it.

findings.title: auth_uid is bound from the JWT, but the display column worker_name is stored exactly as the body supplied it
findings.detail: MEASURED, in the same rolled-back probe that proves this row green. Writing as Hector (JWT sub 8fb252f7-...) while supplying auth_uid = Romeo's id AND worker_name = 'Romeo Beltran': the stored auth_uid was corrected to Hector's by trg_bind_submitter_logbook, and the stored worker_name remained 'Romeo Beltran'. So the authoritative identity is safe and the human-readable one is not. WHY THAT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY, RATHER THAN AS A PURIST POINT: reads across this platform filter and group by worker_name, not by auth_uid - `.eq('worker_name', WORKER_NAME)` is the dominant pattern in logbook, inventory, dayplanner, skillmatrix and the resume evidence path. So a row whose worker_name disagrees with its auth_uid is attributed to the WRONG PERSON in every list that reads it, while looking perfectly consistent to any check that only inspects auth_uid. logbook is the platform's evidence base: it feeds MTBF, PM compliance and a person's resume evidence, so misattribution is not cosmetic. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE because the oracle asks whether identity comes from the JWT rather than the body, and for the identity column it does. TO FINISH: either derive worker_name from auth_uid in the same trigger that already binds auth_uid (it is one lookup away and the trigger is already there), or make the reads key on auth_uid so the display name cannot drive attribution. The first is the smaller change and keeps the existing read patterns working.

findings.title: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 4 of its 6 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - amc_briefings (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); automation_log (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_audit_log (anon 0 rows / m
findings.detail: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 4 of its 6 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - amc_briefings (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); automation_log (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_audit_log (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); parts_staging_recommendations (anon 0 rows / member 1 rows). TO FINISH: this page must decide refusal-vs-absence from SESSION STATE rather than from the response, and its empty state must not claim 'nothing here' when the real answer is 'not signed in'. Of this page's 11 read relation(s), 6 were probed live at the gateway (alert_dismissals, amc_briefings, anomaly_signals, automation_log, hive_audit_log, parts_staging_recommendations).  THE MEASURED FINDING, which is about the CONTRACT rather than a bug: on 26 of the 40 relations a REFUSAL IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ABSENCE. An anonymous caller and an authenticated member receive the SAME status (200) and the same body TYPE (a JSON array), differing only in row count - anon 0 rows, member 2. A request with NO apikey at all also returns 200 []. So nothing in the response separates 'you are not permitted', 'you are not signed in', and 'this hive genuinely has no entries'. This is PostgREST + RLS by construction - row filtering is not request refusal - so it is not a gateway defect. It is an OBLIGATION every surface inherits: the client must decide from session state, and a page that does not will render an expired session as an empty plant. That is the read-path half of the 401-vs-403 lesson this platform already carries. The counter-example proves the point: some relations answer a refusal with 42501, a code a client can act on. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

findings.title: auth_uid is bound from the JWT, but the display column worker_name is stored exactly as the body supplied it
findings.detail: MEASURED, in the same rolled-back probe that proves this row green.
