findings.detail: FAILS at the transport layer, and the obligation lands on this page: 4 of its 6 probed relation(s) return the SAME 200 and the same array body to an anon caller as to a member - amc_briefings (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); automation_log (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); hive_audit_log (anon 0 rows / member 2 rows); parts_staging_recommendations (anon 0 rows / member 1 rows). TO FINISH: this page must decide refusal-vs-absence from SESSION STATE rather than from the response, and its empty state must not claim 'nothing here' when the real answer is 'not signed in'. Of this page's 11 read relation(s), 6 were probed live at the gateway (alert_dismissals, amc_briefings, anomaly_signals, automation_log, hive_audit_log, parts_staging_recommendations).  THE MEASURED FINDING, which is about the CONTRACT rather than a bug: on 26 of the 40 relations a REFUSAL IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ABSENCE. An anonymous caller and an authenticated member receive the SAME status (200) and the same body TYPE (a JSON array), differing only in row count - anon 0 rows, member 2. A request with NO apikey at all also returns 200 []. So nothing in the response separates 'you are not permitted', 'you are not signed in', and 'this hive genuinely has no entries'. This is PostgREST + RLS by construction - row filtering is not request refusal - so it is not a gateway defect. It is an OBLIGATION every surface inherits: the client must decide from session state, and a page that does not will render an expired session as an empty plant. That is the read-path half of the 401-vs-403 lesson this platform already carries. The counter-example proves the point: some relations answer a refusal with 42501, a code a client can act on. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

subject.name: severity means the same here as on hive/analytics

scenarios.oracle: severity vocabulary is one vocabulary shared with hive and analytics - critical here is critical there

evidence.asserts: There are TWO scales here and that is legitimate; the defect was one stored value wearing two different words. THE SCALES: alerts and risk use critical/high/medium/low (v_alert_truth carries critical+high, v_risk_truth carries all four, and analytics and the alert feed render exactly those), while anomalies use what compute_anomaly_signals actually EMITS - critical, warning, info. Different questions, different ladders, and 'critical' is shared and means critical on every one of them - which is the clause this oracle names. Notably alert-hub does not re-derive severity for staging alerts at all: it adopts the canonical risk_level from v_risk_truth (_riskLevelByAsset) rather than inventing a local one. THE DEFECT: for the same stored value 'info', alert-hub rendered 'INFO' while hive rendered 'Watch', so someone moving between the two boards saw two words for one signal. alert-hub also carried a 'watch' key the function never emits - dead, and colliding conceptually with hive's word. Fixed by giving info the label hive already uses ('Watch' says what to do rather than naming a tier) and deleting the unreachable key.
evidence.checked: Compared three sources rather than two: the DB vocabularies straight from v_alert_truth and v_risk_truth, the severities the anomaly function literally emits (read out of its definition: critical, info, warning - no 'watch'), and the tokens each page RENDERS, collected live from alert-hub, hive and analytics. Case differences were treated as presentational and not as vocabulary drift. The one outlier my body-wide scan surfaced - 'Warning' on hive - was checked in context before being called anything, and it is hive's anomaly-scale map, not a stray UI word.
evidence.value_checked: v_alert_truth: critical, high | v_risk_truth: critical, high, medium, low | compute_anomaly_signals emits: critical, info, warning | rendered - alert-hub [High, critical, high], hive [Critical, HIGH, Low, Warning, critical, low, medium], analytics [Critical, High, Low, Medium, critical] | before: info -> 'INFO' on alert-hub vs 'Watch' on hive, plus a dead 'watch' key | after: info -> 'WATCH' on both, ANOMALY_SEVERITY.watch references = 0

findings.detail: Measured with the locally-built 1.4.3 instrument described on the passing rows of this same oracle, self-tested 24/24 in both directions, over a denominator with 0 abstentions - so these are not artefacts of an unresolved background. span.amc-badge "AMC Daily Brief" at 4.46:1 - short of 4.5 by 0.04. NOT BANKED, and the row stays owed: the fix comes first and the row is earned after, which is the fix-before-bank rule. Two cautions for whoever takes it: first, these are SMALL text at 9.3-12px, exactly the band where WCAG 2.x and APCA disagree most - the APCA row for this page passes, and both oracles are supposed to hold, so the fix must not be to relax either one. Second, the same sweep produced one FABRICATED severe failure before the instrument was corrected (dayplanner's clip-text logo read as white-on-orange at 1.72:1), so each of these should be confirmed against its own computed style before any token is changed. resume's 28 all sit at exactly 3.92:1 against rgb(29,43,62), which is the signature of ONE shared muted-text token rather than 28 separate decisions - a single central fix, in the shape of the platform-wide ::placeholder and wayfinding-chip fixes already made in this arc.

findings.title: MEASURED INSIDE THIS VIEW, with tools/prove_view_contrast.mjs - 34 of 37 drivable registry views carried text to measure, ZERO failing.
findings.detail: MEASURED INSIDE THIS VIEW, with tools/prove_view_contrast.mjs - 34 of 37 drivable registry views carried text to measure, ZERO failing. ★WHY A VIEW-SCOPED PROVER HAD TO BE BUILT FOR THIS: a page-level sweep of all 22 pages (tools/prove_page_contrast.mjs) found the platform clean and settled NOTHING here, because every owed contrast row in these banks is authored against V2 or V3 - the dialogs - while their V1 siblings were already green. Banking a page-default reading onto a V2 row is the one-measurement-swept-two-views error that has already put 14 rows in this bank carrying another view's verdict. The view is opened through tools/dialog_targets.mjs, the same shared registry ten other provers use, so the view graded here is the view they grade. WCAG 2.x is measured with the composited probe: the background is blended UP the ancestor chain, because a translucent tint over a dark card is not the colour the stylesheet names, and text over a gradient is recorded as UNMEASURABLE rather than being compared against a canvas it never sits on - the shape that once reported ratio exactly 1.00 for perfectly legible text. NOT BANKED: this view yielded ZERO measurable samples (17 unmeasurable), so there is no denominator and a pass would be vacuous. The cause is structural rather than a probe fault, and it was verified by tracing the paint chain: the dialog's inner card is a TRANSLUCENT GRADIENT - linear-gradient(145deg, rgba(42,61,88,0.6) ...) - over a rgba(0,0,0,0.75) scrim over the page. WCAG 2.x is a ratio between TWO colours, and there is no single background colour here to be the second one. THE APCA SIBLING OF THIS ROW IS NOT AFFECTED and was measured normally, because that lens averages the gradient's stops instead of demanding one flat colour - which is why the platform treats APCA as the primary contrast oracle on this dark shell. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: sample the RENDERED PIXELS around each glyph from a screenshot of this view, which is the only way to obtain the real second colour behind text that sits on a gradient. That is a buildable instrument, not a ceiling - it is simply not built yet, and this row stays owed until it is.

observed.blocker: translucent gradient card over a translucent scrim - no single bg colour exists

evidence.asserts: after dismissing an alert, the surface names what changes and for whom
evidence.checked: LIVE WALK. The confirmation read: 'Alert marked handled -> hidden for your whole hive now, recorded under your name.' It names the effect (the alert is hidden), the SCOPE (the whole hive), the timing ('now') and the attribution. THE FINDING ON THIS VIEW IS THE SCOPE OF A DISMISSAL, and it is the one failure mode the roadmap names for this page: one person quietly blinding the team. Two facts the code states on the same statement: the write is an upsert into alert_dismissals keyed onConflict: 'hive_id,alert_key' - so a dismissal is HIVE state, not personal state, and marking an alert handled removes it from EVERY teammate's inbox - and it records actor: WORKER_NAME, so the action is attributable. The shipped confirmation said only 'Alert marked handled'. It never mentioned either. Someone tidying what they thought was their own view could blind the whole crew to a plant alert and be told nothing. FIXED THIS WALK, claiming only what those two fields back: 'Alert marked handled -> hidden for your whole hive now, recorded under your name.' and, for the snooze branch, '... hidden for your whole hive until then, under your name.' Naming the attribution out loud is what makes the scope read as deliberate rather than accidental. The scope itself was NOT changed - hive-wide dismissal is the right design for shared plant alerts; what was wrong was that the surface never said so. MY VOCABULARY HAD TO BE WIDENED TO GRADE IT, and the gap was real: every NEXT form it knew was ADDITIVE - feeds, counts toward, appears in, visible to - so a sentence whose effect is a REMOVAL scored as naming no following step. A vocabulary that can only recognise things being added cannot grade the surfaces where the risk is something disappearing, which is exactly this one. Reached through the page's own delegated handler, targeting the MARK-HANDLED branch specifically: .alert-dismiss branches three ways by data attribute (data-seen-key acknowledges, data-snooze-key snoozes seven days, a bare data-dismiss-key marks handled), and only the last writes alert_dismissals. The probe stamps an id on the control it found so the press has a stable target rather than re-querying a re-rendered feed.

findings.title: FAILS: with 17 of this page's reads answered 403/42501, it says NOTHING AT ALL - the body text is 4640 characters before the refusal and 848 after, and no new sentence explains anything.  WHAT THIS ORACLE IS REALLY FOR, and the good news first: it checks that a refusal names PERMISSION rather than I
findings.detail: FAILS: with 17 of this page's reads answered 403/42501, it says NOTHING AT ALL - the body text is 4640 characters before the refusal and 848 after, and no new sentence explains anything.  WHAT THIS ORACLE IS REALLY FOR, and the good news first: it checks that a refusal names PERMISSION rather than IDENTITY, because this platform has already shipped that exact inversion - a 42501 rendered as 'your session has expired', which sends a signed-IN person to re-authenticate for a problem authentication cannot fix, and 401/403 collapsed into one message so neither audience got a true statement. ZERO of the 16 graded pages made that mistake on this run. utils.js:1607 whIsAuthFailure() is why: it returns FALSE for status 403 with the comment 'authenticated, and refused. Not a session problem', and documents 42501 as insufficient_privilege. That discrimination is holding. HOW THE REFUSAL WAS INDUCED, and why it is the real branch: every Supabase REST read is answered with the body PostgREST actually sends for a row-level-security refusal - HTTP 403 with {"code":"42501","message":"permission denied for table"} - so the page's own error handling takes the same path it would in production. The patch is on window.fetch, NOT page.route, because a warm service worker serves from cache and bypasses route interception; it is installed with addInitScript in a context closed after each page so it cannot leak. NON-WRITING: it makes a READ return 403. THE INJECTION PROVES ITSELF: every intercepted call increments a counter, and a page where the counter is zero is UNGRADED rather than judged. That guard exists because the first version of this prover silently did nothing - a regex written inside a template literal collapsed to one that terminates at its second character, so the init script was a SyntaxError, every read succeeded normally, and the prover reported 'the reads were all refused and the page said nothing' while nothing had been refused at all. Hit counts on this run ranged from 8 to 42 per page. AND THE SIGNAL MUST APPEAR: the same page is read WITHOUT the injection first, and if its ordinary copy already matches the refusal vocabulary the page is UNGRADED - which is exactly what happened to skillmatrix, whose normal text contains a matching phrase. Without that control a page whose everyday copy happens to say 'cannot' would pass for free. THE SYNTHESIS - THIS IS ONE MISSING SURFACE, NOT 15 PAGE BUGS. Of 16 graded pages: 13 said NOTHING AT ALL when every read was refused, 2 showed only a GENERIC error ('Analysis failed, check console'; 'Achievements failed to load.'), and 1 passed. The platform already has the pieces - a central WRITE-failure message and the correct 401-vs-403 discriminator in utils.js - but there is no equivalent on the READ path, so a refused read renders as dashes or blanks with no explanation. On logbook the numbers '516 entries 30 machines 6 open' became '- entries - machines - open' with the body text identical to the character (1107 before and after) and not one word about why. A person cannot tell 'there is no data' from 'the load failed' from 'you are not allowed', and those three call for three different actions. THE FIX IS ONE ADOPTION, not 15 edits: give the read path the same treatment the write path already has. This independently reproduces a finding already recorded as 'the message already exists; the gap is ADOPTION on the read path'. SCOPE: V1, the page as it loads, and READ refusal only - a refused WRITE is a different path with its own central message, and is not claimed here. 5 of the 22 pages are excluded from the sweep because they are public or have no authenticated read to refuse. The walk is NON-WRITING.

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_journey.mjs --journeys j5, walked live: 16 composer(s) across the roster, ZERO failing.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_journey.mjs --journeys j5, walked live: 16 composer(s) across the roster, ZERO failing. THE JOURNEY: type into a composer, get called away, come back - and nothing may have half-landed. It is the most ordinary thing that happens to someone on a plant floor, and the failure it hunts is a page that treats abandoned input as a committed record. ★THE DISCRIMINATION THAT MAKES THE VERDICT FAIR, and without which this oracle would punish good behaviour: after the reload the marker text is looked for in TWO places, and they mean opposite things. Back inside the COMPOSER FIELD means a DRAFT was deliberately preserved - that is good UX and passes. Out in the page's own CONTENT means it half-landed, and a person who typed and walked away now owns a record they never submitted - that fails. A checker that merely searched the page for the text would call the good case and the bad case the same thing. NON-WRITING BY CONSTRUCTION: nothing is ever submitted; the marker only ever reaches an input's value, so this prover cannot pollute the shared test database. The composer inventory comes from tools/dialog_targets.mjs - the same grounded registry four other provers read - so which views count as composers cannot drift from how those views are known to open.FOR THIS PAGE AND PERSONA THERE IS NOTHING TO ABANDON. The prover walked all 66 (page, persona) pairs and reached a composer on 16 of them; this pair reported no composer at all, so the journey could not be CONSTRUCTED. ★THAT IS RECORDED AS UNBUILT, NOT AS A PASS, and the distinction is the whole point: a journey that cannot be constructed must never be scored green, because 'nothing half-landed' is trivially true of a surface where nothing can be typed. The prover carries that rail explicitly - non-vacuity, a journey that cannot be built is a finding rather than a quiet skip - and banking it green would be the empty-denominator failure this bank exists to catch. WHY THIS PAIR HAS NONE: the composer inventory is tools/dialog_targets.mjs, and a composer is only counted when it is reachable FOR THIS IDENTITY. index's fields, for instance, live on the anon landing and the sign-in modal, so a signed-in persona has no composer on that page even though the page plainly contains inputs. A read-only surface (public-feed, achievements, the report pages) has none for any persona. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: either this pair genuinely has a composer the registry does not yet list - in which case the registry gains an entry and the prover reaches it - or the row is dispositioned declared-na under R10 with 'this surface has nothing to abandon' as the reason and the page's own CO recovery oracles as the replacement. Left owed rather than declared here, because deciding which of those two it is needs the per-page composer question answered, not assumed.

On this page the person-caused action is dismissing an alert, which is ONE press - there is no part-way. You either pressed it or you did not, so there is no half-applied state to leave behind and no draft to return to. ★WHY THIS IS RECORDED RATHER THAN PASSED: 'no half-applied state' over an action with no middle is VACUOUSLY TRUE, and a vacuous truth banked as a live-walk PASS is how coverage improves by deleting obligations. Fourteen OTHER surfaces on this platform DO have a midway - a capture modal, a composer, a multi-field form - and all fourteen were driven, filled and abandoned by reload. This page is not one of them, and the emptiness is the finding. ★THE REPLACEMENT, so the surface is not simply excused: what this page owes instead is that the effect its one press DOES cause is observable to the person who caused it - carried by effect_visible, already proven green here (PB-alert-hub-072-CF-ufai-F-V1-effect_visible). A one-press surface is still accountable; it is accountable for a different sentence. ★AND ONE PAGE WAS DELIBERATELY EXCLUDED FROM THIS DISPOSITION: skillmatrix has no green effect_visible, because its exam could not be reached (SKILL_CONTENT is module-scoped and no discipline/level pair produced questions). Declaring NA there would excuse an obligation against a replacement that does not exist, which is the same vacuity wearing R10's clothes. Its rows stay owed with that diagnosis.

The run was killed twice - once by my own 570-second timeout and once when the backgrounded process lost its browser - and BOTH times it emitted those as FAILs. A probe whose browser is shot out from under it reports every remaining page as broken. ★SO THEY ARE NOT BANKED. Fifty false reds would have read as the worst finding of the session, and the only thing separating them from a real one is that I read the verdict string instead of the count. Re-WALKED, never re-baselined.

findings.detail: FAILS: UNEXPLAINED EMPTY — 10 number(s), all zero/blank, and nothing on screen says the data could not be loaded. With a session this view rendered 10 non-zero value(s) over 4728 characters; with the auth token removed from storage it rendered 0 over 901, and the page did not redirect, did not add a sign-in prompt it was not already showing, and did not state that anything failed to load. What is on screen after the kill: "Skip to main content Alert Hub Everything that needs your attention, in one place. Live data · Based on your risk scores · PM overdue: counted once per asset, matches PM ".  WHY THIS FINDING IS WORDED NARROWLY, and what it deliberately does NOT claim: the obvious reading - 'the page should have redirected or announced an ended session' - is WRONG on this platform, and checking that is what kept this row honest. index.html:3520 shows a designed branch for 'Guest worker (has name, no auth session)' which shows an upgrade nudge, and index.html:902-906 stamps its wh-signed-in paint-hint from wh_last_worker + wh_active_hive_id in localStorage precisely so a known user does not watch the marketing landing collapse into the dashboard (a measured CLS of 0.24). So a cached identity with no session is a SUPPORTED state here, not a defect, and demanding a redirect would have manufactured one. What is not defensible is the other half: hive-scoped reads that could not have succeeded rendering as zeros with nothing saying so. On index that surfaces as the words 'ALL CLEAR - Nothing urgent right now' beside the real hive name - an affirmative safety claim derived from a read that never happened, which is the same shape as the two moderation badges that asserted '0 waiting' on a failed read. HOW IT WAS MEASURED, live, and what the oracle deliberately is NOT: it is not 'does the page redirect to sign-in'. Several of these surfaces are legitimately readable signed-out, so a redirect is only ONE honest answer and demanding it would manufacture defects on the public pages. The oracle is the NEGATIVE: a page must never present a signed-out state as though it were signed-in data. Three behaviours are accepted and the row NAMES which one this page did - (1) redirect to a sign-in surface or render a sign-in prompt it was not rendering before, (2) render an empty state that STATES its reason, (3) be a genuinely public surface that renders identical content either way. What FAILS is the fourth: hive-scoped numbers still on screen, or bare zeros and dashes with no explanation, standing in for a read that could not have succeeded. THE SESSION IS KILLED IN localStorage, NOT IN COOKIES, and that detail is the difference between a real measurement and a vacuous one: supabase-js persists the session as sb-<project-ref>-auth-token in localStorage, so clearing cookies would leave the page fully signed in and the probe would measure nothing while reporting a pass. Every sb-* / auth-token / supabase key in BOTH localStorage and sessionStorage is swept (hardcoding one project ref is the other way this goes silently vacuous), then the page is RELOADED so the client re-reads storage from cold. THE CONTROL IS THE SIGNED-IN READING, TAKEN FIRST: the same page is measured with a session, and the two readings must differ. A probe that cannot prove it changed anything cannot report that the change was handled correctly - so a page that looks identical either way is either genuinely public (case 3, and then it must show no hive-scoped values at all) or the kill did not take, and those two are never allowed to be confused: the second is recorded UNGRADED, never as a pass. TWO FALSE READINGS WERE CAUGHT AND FIXED BEFORE ANYTHING WAS BANKED, and both are why this row is trustworthy. FIRST, THE PROVER REPORTED A PASS OVER AN EMPTY DENOMINATOR: the text-matching regexes were declared in Node scope but referenced inside the page.evaluate callback, which runs in the BROWSER, so every page threw ReferenceError and came back UNGRADED - and the summary printed 'PASS - no page presents a dead session as signed-in data', true only in the sense that no page had been looked at. Zero failures over zero measurements is now an explicit FAIL, louder than a real failure, because a failure gets triaged while a vacuous green gets banked. SECOND, A BODY-WIDE KEYWORD MATCH READ THE PAGE'S OWN MARKETING COPY AS EVIDENCE: public-feed was credited with 'says-signed-out' because its text matched /sign in/ - but it matched BEFORE the kill too, since the page permanently renders 'Sign In ->' and 'Sign in to join the conversation' as its read-only CTA, and its body was byte-identical either way at 2438 characters with zero non-zero values both times. A signed-out sentence now only counts if it APPEARED after the kill, and the unchanged/public case is tested BEFORE any text match rather than after it - which is how public-feed came to be recorded as what it actually is, a public surface, rather than as a page that announced a dead session. THIRD, A LEAK SUB-CHECK WAS BUILT AND THEN DELIBERATELY DEMOTED TO INFORMATIONAL, because it could not tell leaked USER data from static FURNITURE and it got that wrong in BOTH directions. Comparing the signed-in and signed-out readings for values that survived, it called index a leak on a bare '3' with no class - a coincidence between a step indicator and a tile - and then, after being tightened to require a class and more than one digit, it called achievements a leak on 18/38/63/83 .wh-avatar-lvl, which are the Iron/Bronze/Silver/Gold tier THRESHOLDS: identical for every user and CORRECT to survive a signed-out reload. Telling those apart requires knowing which numbers are user-scoped, which no generic DOM read can answer, so claiming it anyway would be manufacturing findings. The oracle now grades ONLY the classification it can actually establish, and the survivor list travels with the row as context for a human rather than as a verdict. FOURTH, THE FAILING VERDICT MISDESCRIBED ITS OWN MEASUREMENT: it read 'N number(s), all zero/blank' on every page that reached that branch, while achievements had 6 of 9 non-zero. A verdict that contradicts its own reading is the mislabelled-metric defect wearing a test's clothes; it now states the counts it measured. FIFTH, A PAGE STILL LOADING WAS BEING REPORTED AS A PAGE THAT FAILED TO EXPLAIN ITSELF. The sweep called asset-hub, analytics and shift-brain UNEXPLAINED EMPTY with ZERO numbers on screen - but zero numbers is equally the signature of a page that had not finished rendering 3.4 seconds after a reload, which is the SLOW-vs-STUCK distinction the component-states prover already had to learn. A page that looks under-rendered, or is still showing aria-busy / skeleton / spinner elements, now gets another 6 seconds and is re-read; if it is still unsettled the row is UNGRADED rather than failed, because the reading genuinely cannot tell the two apart. SIXTH, THE ORACLE WAS FAILING PAGES THAT HAVE NO SUBJECT. assistant and report-sender rendered ZERO non-zero values even WITH a session - a chat thread and an empty report list - so there is no figure on either page that a dead session could turn into a false reassurance. Failing them would be asserting a defect in the absence of the thing the assertion is about, so a page with no data signed-in is now UNGRADED with that reason recorded. Across six corrections the pattern is the same one this whole bank keeps teaching: the instrument was wrong more often than the pages were, and every one of these was caught by reading what the page actually rendered instead of trusting the verdict. SEVENTH, THE READINESS GUARD ITSELF WAS TOO BLUNT AND DISQUALIFIED FINISHED PAGES. Counting elements matching skeleton/spinner/aria-busy selectors by SELECTOR ALONE flipped public-feed from a correct pass to UNGRADED on 1 busy element at 2473 rendered characters, and did the same to engineering-design (3 at 1851) and report-sender (2 at 1176) - because pages routinely leave a skeleton node in the DOM with display:none once the real content arrives. A hidden skeleton is a template, not a loading state, so only VISIBLE busy elements count. EIGHTH, A PASSING VERDICT NAMED A MECHANISM IT HAD NOT ESTABLISHED: an unchanged page with no figures was labelled 'public-surface-identical-signed-out' and PASSED, which called project-report - a hive report page - a public surface purely because it renders no numbers in either state. Every PASS must now rest on POSITIVE evidence (a redirect, a prompt that appeared, a sentence that appeared, a stated reason for being empty); an unchanged reading and a view with no figures at all are both UNGRADED, with the reason recorded, so they stay owed rather than being banked on a label nobody proved. WHAT IS NOT PROVEN: this is V1, the page as it loads, and it settles the CLIENT's behaviour when the stored session is gone. It does not test an EXPIRED-but-present token (a different path: the server refuses and the client must translate that refusal), nor a session that dies mid-action while a write is in flight. Those are separate oracles and stay owed rather than inheriting this reading. The walk is NON-WRITING - it reads, clears client-side storage in its own browser context, and reloads - so it cannot have touched the shared test database.

findings.title: LEFT OWED with a diagnosis, because this view is unreachable on this hive for a DATA reason and a disposition would be a claim about the view rather than about the data.
findings.detail: LEFT OWED with a diagnosis, because this view is unreachable on this hive for a DATA reason and a disposition would be a claim about the view rather than about the data. MEASURED: #amc-card ships display:none and never became visible within 12s - the reach THREW rather than enumerating an invisible container as an empty view. The database explains it exactly: amc_briefings holds 11 rows for this hive but the newest is shift_date 2026-08-17, with statuses expired/pending - so there is no brief for TODAY, and the card is correctly hidden. THE VIEW DOES COMMIT WHEN IT EXISTS, which is why this cannot be declared-na: the hidden card's own markup carries 'Approve brief' and 'Reject' - an approval pair, and approvals are the class this platform treats as online-only-with-clarity. Those are the actions these three oracles need to grade, and they cannot be reached without a brief. AND THE PAGE HANDLES THE ABSENCE WELL, recorded so the next walker does not mistake this for a defect: the summary hero reads 'AMC daily brief / None today / No AMC brief for today's shift / NO BRIEF', which distinguishes an ABSENT brief from a brief with zero items - the exact distinction its sibling anomaly card was failing (see V1's finding). WHAT THE NEXT WALK NEEDS: a briefing for today. Two routes, in order of honesty - let the analytics-orchestrator generate one on open (the path the product uses), or insert an amc_briefings row with today's shift_date and status pending. Then walk Approve and Reject: whether approval is idempotent (one brief per hive per day), whether the approver is named on the row, and whether a rejected brief says what happens next.

observed.absence_handled_well: hero reads 'None today / No AMC brief for today's shift / NO BRIEF'
observed.seed_route: orchestrator generates on open, or insert an amc_briefings row for today

findings.title: LEFT OWED with a CORRECTED diagnosis - the third version, and the two wrong ones are recorded because each was a plausible false finding.
findings.detail: LEFT OWED with a CORRECTED diagnosis - the third version, and the two wrong ones are recorded because each was a plausible false finding. FIRST I SAID: no brief exists for today, so the card hides. SECOND I SAID: that was wrong, a pending unexpired brief for today DOES exist (shift_date 2026-08-17, status pending, expires_at 2026-08-18 10:00Z) and the card hiding it means a supervisor can never approve it - a real defect. THAT WAS ALSO WRONG, and the reason is worth the space: I was reading the DATABASE's current_date (2026-08-17, UTC-based) as the application's day. WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE, traced on the wire. The client queries shift_date=eq.<todayPhtIso()> and sent eq.2026-08-18, because shift_date on this platform is defined as timezone('Asia/Manila', now())::date and the helper's own comment says it builds the same value so the filter matches exactly. Manila was already 2026-08-18 02:18 while UTC was 2026-08-17 18:18. The stored brief is correctly stamped: generated_at 2026-08-16 22:00Z is 06:00 Manila on the 17th, so shift_date 2026-08-17 is right. Briefs are generated around 06:00 Manila daily, and it was 02:18 - so no brief for Manila-today exists YET. Client correct, row correct, card correctly hidden, and the hero's 'None today / NO BRIEF' is correct too. NOT a defect. THE ONE REAL QUESTION THIS EXPOSED, recorded rather than claimed: yesterday's brief is still PENDING and unexpired, and the approval pair ('Approve brief' / 'Reject') lives on the TODAY card only - the historic query explicitly fetches neq.today rows. So a brief not approved before the Manila day rolls over may become unapprovable, and it would sit pending forever with nothing surfacing it. Whether the historic list offers approval is NOT established here and must be read rather than assumed - if it does not, that is a genuine stranded-approval defect on an approval-class write. WHAT THE NEXT WALK NEEDS: run between 06:00 and midnight Manila so a brief for the current Manila date exists, then walk Approve and Reject - checking idempotency (the DB enforces one brief per hive per shift_date via uq_amc_briefings_hive_shift, which is this page's own invariant already held at the database), whether the approver is named on the row, and what a rejection says happens next. Do NOT seed by inserting a second row for the same date; the unique constraint will refuse it, correctly.

observed.verdict: not a defect - no brief for Manila-today exists yet
observed.my_two_wrong_diagnoses: (1) no brief exists (2) a pending brief is unreachable - both from reading the DB current_date as the app day
observed.real_open_question: a pending brief may become unapprovable after the Manila day rolls over - approval pair is on the today card only
observed.db_invariant_confirmed: uq_amc_briefings_hive_shift enforces one brief per hive per shift_date
observed.do_not_seed: a second row for the same date is refused by the unique constraint, correctly

findings.title: STILL OWED - the approve/reject pair cannot be reached on this hive today - but THE OPEN QUESTION THIS ROW RECORDED IS NOW ANSWERED, and the answer was the bad one.
findings.detail: STILL OWED - the approve/reject pair cannot be reached on this hive today - but THE OPEN QUESTION THIS ROW RECORDED IS NOW ANSWERED, and the answer was the bad one. The previous diagnosis said: 'Whether the historic list offers approval is NOT established here and must be read rather than assumed - if it does not, that is a genuine stranded-approval defect on an approval-class write.' READ (alert-hub.html ~1359-1372): it does not. Historic briefs are pushed into the alert feed with actionLabel: '' - no action affordance at all - and the severity map sent anything not rejected/expired, INCLUDING pending, to 'info', the lowest rung. evidence.asserts: a dismissal that cannot be saved never silently hides the alert - the optimistic removal is rolled back and the alert is restored with a message - and a dismissal that DOES save says plainly what it did and to whom, so a wrong action is recoverable rather than invisible
evidence.checked: Read at the call site after a live probe produced a misleading absence, and the code path is what resolved it. MY LIVE READING WAS WRONG TWICE AND THE PAGE IS RIGHT: probing with writes stubbed, I saw 29 snooze controls, ZERO undo affordances, ZERO announcements even with a MutationObserver armed before the click, and tab counts unchanged at 'All 61' - which reads as an irreversible action with no feedback. It is the opposite. alert-hub.html:1534 refuses the whole dismissal via whRequireOnline BEFORE the optimistic mutation, so in an environment that cannot reach the network nothing is removed, nothing is written and there is nothing to undo - my harness looked exactly like that environment. THE RECOVERY BEHAVIOUR IS EXPLICIT IN BOTH DIRECTIONS: on failure the catch at :1561-1566 deletes the optimistic dismissal, restores the previous alert list (_alerts = prev), re-renders, and says 'Could not save, alert restored' - so a write that dies cannot leave a plant alert quietly hidden, which the comment at :1529-1533 records as a real past defect fixed here. On success the toast states the SCOPE and the ATTRIBUTION: 'Snoozed for N days -> hidden for your whole hive until then, under your name.' That sentence is the correction affordance that matters on a shared inbox - a person who snoozes wrongly is told immediately that they hid it for everyone and that the row carries their name (actor: WORKER_NAME, upserted onConflict hive_id,alert_key), so the mistake is visible and attributable rather than silent. Read-only: alert_dismissals held 0 rows before this work and holds 0 rows after, verified by re-count - no dismissal was written to the shared database.
